newsitem.title: INDIA: Hindu party ready to form Indian state government.
newsitem.headline: Hindu party ready to form Indian state government.

text.p: The Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) prepared to form a minority government in Uttar Pradesh on Tuesday after inconclusive state polls, politicians said.
The BJP emerged with 177 seats in the state's 425-member lower house after three-phase polls which ended last week.

That was well short of the outright majority the right-wing party had sought to help propel it to national power. However, a bitter struggle between the two other main political parties in the state could give the BJP an opening to take control.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition, led by federal defence minister Mulayam Singh Yadav, ended with 134 members in the hung assembly, the largest single group after the BJP.
The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) of former chief minister Mayawati (Eds: one name), representing the lowest Hindu castes, won 67 seats, while its Congress party ally clinched 33.
But the BSP and Yadav's socialist Samajwadi Party, Deve Gowda's key alliance partner in Uttar Pradesh, have refused to join forces.

On Monday, the BSP, which had staked its claim to form a government, abruptly said it would sit in the opposition ranks after failing to gain the support of the United Front, which backs Yadav for the chief minister's job.

BJP officials said they were preparing to meet Uttar Pradesh Governor Romesh Bhandari, who must swear in a government before October 17, when New Delhi's authority to exercise direct federal rule over the state expires.
The BJP's nominee for chief minister, Kalyan Singh, told Reuters his party had mustered enough supporters to win a vote of confidence if Bhandari did invite him to form the government.
"Let the governor extend an invitation to us on the basis of our being the single largest party and we will prove our majority on the floor of the house," Singh said in the state capital of Lucknow.
The BJP regards Uttar Pradesh as the launchpad for a bid to replace India's traditionally centre-left secular governments in New Delhi with a hardline Hindu nationalist government.

The BJP's campaign to build a Hindu temple at the site of a 16th century mosque in Ayodhya in the heart of Uttar Pradesh catapulted it from a mere two seats in parliament in the 1984 elections to becoming India's main opposition party in 1991.

It briefly held power in the state in 1991. But after Hindu zealots demolished the Babri mosque in Ayodhya in December 1992, former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao sacked four BJP state governments, including the one ruling Uttar Pradesh.
The United Front's decision-making Steering Committee was due to meet later on Tuesday to decide if Yadav would stake a claim to form the government.

"At the moment, it looks like the BJP has the edge as the largest party," a United Front politician confessed. But he added that a surprise meeting between Congress President Sitaram Kesri and Deve Gowda later on Tuesday could change the equation.

"There is a feeling among Congressmen that no effort should be spared to keep the BJP out," a Congress spokesman told Reuters after Kesri met Deve Gowda and headed for a meeting with other United Front leaders.
"Mr Kesri's meeting with Mr Deve Gowda and the United Front leaders would discuss this issue," the spokesman said.
